teaser.en: Children hunt its masses of tiny white berries, while their parents cut its twigs to build granaries and fish traps.

summary.en: *Mkpwamba* is the white-berry bush, a much-branched shrub covered in small white berries. Its fruit feeds children, its twigs build houses, granaries and fish traps, and its root bark is used against malaria.

about.en: *Mkpwamba* is a much-branched shrub, usually 1 to 3 m tall, with red-brown stems and small, neat leaves. In fruit it is covered in masses of small white berries, so many that the bush can look dusted with snow.

where.en: It is common throughout the coast, in bushland, thicket and fallow fields. The white berries make it easy to spot.

uses.en: The white berries are eaten by children. The long, thin twigs are used in building houses and granaries and in making fish traps. The Digo of Diani boil the root bark to treat malaria.

culture.en: The Digo distinguish a 'female' and a 'male' *mkpwamba*. This white-fruited plant is the female; the male is a related shrub, *Phyllanthus reticulatus*.

names.en: Pakia records *mkpwamba*, with the forms *mkpwamba mchetu* and *mkpwamba vitu*, and also *mkambakamba*. ICRAF's handbook writes *mkwamba*, which is also the Swahili, Giriama and Chonyi name; Swahili also has *mteja*. In English it is the white-berry bush.

reason.en: Tassel berry, same family and also has edible berries
Bush shrub whose root bark is also boiled for malaria
Another bush shrub with fruit eaten by children

sources: Pakia, M. (2005) African Traditional Plant Knowledge Today: an ethnobotanical study of the Digo at the Kenya Coast. PhD thesis, Univ. Bayreuth, Appendix III (Digo–botanical name list) & Appendix VI (name semantics). https://epub.uni-bayreuth.de/881/1/Pakia.pdf
